# Shipping stocks: how to analyze shipping companies

**Shipping stocks are shares in companies selling transport on a world market that prices it daily in dollars, while production — the vessel — lives for twenty-five years and cannot be switched off.** Nowhere else is revenue this mobile united with an asset this sluggish. The mechanisms are gathered in [the course on shipping](/kurser/se-18-rederi-och-shipping); AK1A's universe holds the Nordic core: Maersk, the line owning its fleet, DSV, the forwarder hiring capacity — an owner-against-hirer contrast.

## The freight rate — shipping stocks' priced world

Sea freight's price is the freight rate, set where supply meets demand: vessels seeking cargo, cargoes seeking vessels. The fleet can neither grow in weeks nor be laid up — a vessel lying still loses crew, classification and contracts, sailing on until the price has fallen enough. The course's witness is the dry bulk index 2008: 11,793 in May on China's raw-material hunger, 663 in December after the crisis's cargo collapse — quotient 663 ÷ 11,793 = 0.056, just below six percent of the peak after seven months. [Cycle risk](/kurser/rk-05-cykelrisk), pure and simple. The market side belongs to [the commodity cycle guide](/blogg/ravarubolag-materialbranschens-cykel); this guide owns the accounting side — and since freight prices in dollars, [currency risk](/kurser/rk-07-valutarisk) sits inside revenue.

## Spot or time charter — the income's valve

On spot, capacity sells by the day at today's price: full cycle wind both ways. A time charter locks vessel and freight for months or years: lower peak, higher floor. The course's practice fleet Nordviks Rederi sails ten vessels, six on charters: the share 6 ÷ 10 = 0.60 is its cycle temperament. The arithmetic: the breakeven point — operations 12,000, financing 8,000, administration 5,000 dollars per day — becomes 12,000 + 8,000 + 5,000 = 25,000. The boom's spot of 80,000 gives a contribution of 80,000 − 25,000 = 55,000 dollars per day; over 300 operating days 55,000 × 300 = 16,500,000 per vessel and year. The trough's spot of 18,000 gives 18,000 − 25,000 = −7,000 per day and −7,000 × 300 = −2,100,000 per vessel — for the ten-vessel fleet, 21 million dollars bleeding, year after year. The charter mix 0.6 × 35,000 + 0.4 × 18,000 = 28,200 dollars per day holds the same fleet above breakeven: 28,200 − 25,000 = 3,200 per day, 3,200 × 300 = 960,000 per vessel and year. Same market, same vessels — the mix decides wipeout or survival.

## Operating leverage — the fixed costs' magnifier

Crew, insurance, maintenance, classification and interest are fixed whatever the freight rate; every price movement is magnified en route to the result — [the cost coverage unit](/kurser/mt-06-kostnadsoverlagsenhet)'s mechanics at their extreme. The yardstick: the quotient freight rate ÷ (freight rate − breakeven). For the charter rate 35,000 with contribution 35,000 − 25,000 = 10,000, it becomes 35,000 ÷ 10,000 = 3.5. If the freight rate falls ten percent, to 31,500, the contribution sinks to 31,500 − 25,000 = 6,500 — minus 35 percent: ten on the price became thirty-five on the result. At the peak the quotient is lower: spot 80,000, contribution 55,000, gives 80,000 ÷ 55,000 = 1.45, and a ten percent fall to 72,000 gives 72,000 − 25,000 = 47,000, minus 14.5 percent. For shipping stocks leverage is the protagonist: small change in the freight rate, large change in profit.

## Supply inertia — the fleet's age and the newbuild orderbook

A newbuilt vessel costs, in the course's exercise, 105 million dollars and two and a half years to build — then lives twenty-five years. Supply's inertia lies there: newbuild contracts are written in boom euphoria, delivered into the next slowdown; a vessel that exists is not scrapped early without giving up its scrap value — in the exercise 15 million dollars. Fleet age and orderbook are the sector's clock: fifteen-year-old vessels with ten years left, the trough's scrapping candidates; a full orderbook, the peak's messenger. The second-hand market likewise: the same five-year-old vessel trades at the top for 110 million dollars, at the bottom for 55 — difference 110 − 55 = 55 million, value halved. At the bottom the oldest vessels near the scrap floor: 15 of 55 million is 27 percent — demolition turns rational, supply is eaten, the cycle turns. The newbuild pipeline is the sector's [business-cycle indicator](/kurser/ma-04-konjunkturindikatorerna); the vessel as asset belongs in [substance quality](/kurser/ib-02-substansens-kvalitet).

## The balance sheet — who survives the valley

Troughs last, and the vessel is heavy, swinging — financing decides who sees the next peak. The course's equation: 105 million in debt against a vessel valued at 55 means the bank owns it, not the analyst. [The balance sheet](/kurser/bk-01-balansrakningen) is therefore read before the income statement, [the debt-to-equity ratio](/blogg/skuldsattningsgrad-vilken-niva-ar-farlig) weighed with [solidity and interest coverage](/kurser/st-01-soliditet-och-rantetackning). The universe's contrast: Maersk 0.31 debt-to-equity including vessel leasing, DSV after the Schenker acquisition 0.76 — the forwarder's balance sheet carries acquisition loans, the line's vessels. DSV's result has fallen every year of the series — 17,568, 12,315, 10,109 and 8,095 million Danish kroner — while free cash flow has stayed positive five years in a row: survival sits in cash as much as profit. Low indebtedness buys the time the cycle turn demands — and time the only certain healer of losses.

## Maersk — the cycle's Nordic textbook

No Nordic company illustrates the freight cycle better than A.P. Møller-Mærsk. Between the financial years 2022 and 2023 revenue fell from 81,529 to 51,065 million dollars — minus 37.4 percent — while the result fell from 29,198 to 3,822 million — minus 86.9 percent. Operating leverage in reality: just over a third of the revenue vanished, almost nine tenths of the result. Thereafter recovery to 6,109 million and 2025's 2,725 million — 9.3 percent of the record year's profit. Universe margins: gross 21.0 percent, operating 9.1, net 4.1 — the fleet's capital cost presses. The dividend of 480 Danish kronor per share yields 2.12 percent on a payout of 47.2 percent — a cycle dividend following the freight, not policy — see [dividend basics](/blogg/utdelningar-101). Neighbour DSV, owned by [the logistics course](/kurser/se-15-logistik), hires capacity at gross margin 26.8 against the line's 21.0: the owner carries the cycle in the balance sheet, the hirer in the contracts.

## Valuation — P/B against P/E in a cyclical industry

P/E is deceived in cyclical industries by the mechanics creating them: the E in the denominator is a freight curve. Maersk trades at P/E 22.2 — not because the market pays for growth, but because the profit sits at the cycle bottom, expected to fall as freight rates normalize: the multiple rises by itself unchanged. [Normalized multiples](/kurser/vr-02-normaliserade-multipler) and [the P/E course's warnings](/kurser/km-009-pe) are standard tools; comparison runs within the family against [sector medians](/blogg/branschmedianer-akm2). P/B captures what P/E misses: the substance. Maersk P/B 0.92 — below one — mirrors a fleet booked at values swinging with the cycle; the five-year-old's journey from 110 to 55 million shows book value is a cycle number, and [the P/B ratio's pitfalls](/blogg/pb-tal-nar-jamfor-man-bokvarde-ratt) ask: second-hand values or old newbuild prices? [The sector analysis method](/kurser/se-16-sektoranalysens-metod) ties it together: revenue engine the freight rate, margin engine the breakeven point, balance the survival question.

## Checklist: six questions when you analyze shipping stocks

1. **The freight rate's position** — where does today's freight stand against a normalized average, and what does supply-demand say?
2. **The charter share** — how large a part of the fleet sails on time charters, at which rates?
3. **The breakeven point** — which daily freight covers operations, financing and administration, and how far above lies today's earning?
4. **Fleet age and orderbook** — how old are the vessels, how many newbuilds ordered ahead?
5. **The debt per vessel** — how much net debt does the balance sheet carry against the fleet's second-hand value?
6. **The valuation measure** — is P/E read normalized against the cycle, and P/B against real second-hand values?

Shipping stocks reward whoever computes the freight rate against breakeven, not guesses at peaks: the earning is weather, but indebtedness, charter mix and fleet age are seamanship — there it is decided who sails on. The whole is gathered in [the complete guide to Swedish stock analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026).
